title: Eating and drinking
goal: Ordering at a cha chaan teng and at yum cha, telling 想 from 要, saying what you like with 鍾意, and asking for the bill with 埋單 — all with sentences people really say in Hong Kong.
bekal: order food and drinks with 要 and 想
tell 食 and 飲 apart — two verbs you must never mix up
say what you like and don't like with 鍾意
order drinks with extras like 走甜, 少冰, 熱
ask for the bill: 唔該埋單

dialogs.title: 對話 1 — At a cha chaan teng
dialogs.intro: Andi and Wong Lai have lunch at a 茶餐廳, the classic Hong Kong diner that serves everything fast. The waiter talks fast and short — that's not rudeness, it's just the style.

lines.speaker: 伙記:
lines.text: [幾多位|Gei2 do1 wai2][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: How many?
lines.literal: how — many — person-classifier — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [兩位|Loeng5 wai2]。
lines.id: Two.
lines.literal: two — person-classifier.

lines.speaker: 伙記:
lines.text: [呢邊坐|Ni1 bin1 co5]。[飲咩呀|Jam2 me1 aa3]？
lines.id: Sit here. What to drink?
lines.literal: this — side — sit. drink — what — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我要|Ngo5 jiu3][一杯凍檸茶|jat1 bui1 dung3 ning4 caa4]，[少甜|siu2 tim4]。
lines.id: I'll have an iced lemon tea, less sweet.
lines.literal: I — want — one — glass — iced — lemon — tea, little — sweet.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [我要|Ngo5 jiu3][熱奶茶|jit6 naai5 caa4]。
lines.id: A hot milk tea for me.
lines.literal: I — want — hot — milk — tea.

lines.speaker: 伙記:
lines.text: [食咩呀|Sik6 me1 aa3]？
lines.id: What to eat?
lines.literal: eat — what — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我想食|Ngo5 soeng2 sik6][叉燒飯|caa1 siu1 faan6]。
lines.id: I'd like char siu rice.
lines.literal: I — would-like — eat — char-siu — rice.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [我要|Ngo5 jiu3][一碗雲吞麵|jat1 wun2 wan4 tan1 min6]，[唔該|m4 goi1]。
lines.id: A bowl of wonton noodles for me, please.
lines.literal: I — want — one — bowl — wonton — noodle, please.

lines.speaker: 伙記:
lines.text: [好|Hou2]，[等陣呀|dang2 zan6 aa3]。
lines.id: OK, just a moment.
lines.literal: good, wait — a-moment — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [嘩|Waa4]，[好好味|hou2 hou2 mei6][呀|aa3]！
lines.id: Wow, this is so good!
lines.literal: wow, filler — good — taste — huh.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [我食飽喇|Ngo5 sik6 baau2 laa3]。[唔該埋單|M4 goi1 maai4 daan1]！
lines.id: I'm full. The bill, please!
lines.literal: I — eat — full — already. please — close — bill.

lines.speaker: 伙記:
lines.text: [一共|Jat1 gung6][一百二十蚊|jat1 baak3 ji6 sap6 man1]，[多謝|do1 ze6]。
lines.id: That's a hundred and twenty altogether, thank you.
lines.literal: one — together — one — hundred — two — ten — dollar, thanks.

notes: **⚠️ [食|sik6] is for food, [飲|jam2] is for drinks — and they're never swapped.** These are native Cantonese words; Mandarin uses 吃 and 喝. [食飯|sik6 faan6] = eat (a meal); [飲茶|jam2 caa4] = drink tea. 🇭🇰 Note that 食 also covers things that aren't food in English: [食煙|sik6 jin1] = smoke, [食藥|sik6 joek6] = take medicine.

**[伙記|fo2 gei3] is what you call a waiter at a diner**, and you're free to use it. 🇭🇰 But the safest and most common way is just one word: [唔該|M4 goi1]！ said a bit loudly. That's enough to call anyone anywhere in Hong Kong.

**[少甜|siu2 tim4] and its relatives are the secret language of the cha chaan teng.** [少甜|siu2 tim4] = less sugar; [走甜|zau2 tim4] = no sugar at all; [少冰|siu2 bing1] = light ice; [走冰|zau2 bing1] = no ice; [飛邊|fei1 bin1] = bread with crusts off. [走|zau2] literally means “leave”, and on a menu it means “remove”.
**[等陣|dang2 zan6] = just a moment.** You'll hear it every time you order anything. Other forms just as common: [等一陣|dang2 jat1 zan6] and [等陣間|dang2 zan6 gaan1].

**[好味|hou2 mei6] = tasty, and notice that 好 appears twice in [好好味|hou2 hou2 mei6].** The first is the required filler you know from Unit 1; the second is part of the word 好味 itself. So 好好味 = “really tasty”, not a typo.

**[埋單|maai4 daan1] = ask for the bill.** Literally “close the list”. ⚠️ In Mandarin this became 買單, with the character for “buy” — a mix-up born from mishearing. The correct Cantonese form is 埋單, and 埋 here means “bring together, close”.
**[飽|baau2] = full, [肚餓|tou5 ngo6] = hungry.** Both take 好: [我好肚餓|Ngo5 hou2 tou5 ngo6] = I'm really hungry. [我食飽喇|Ngo5 sik6 baau2 laa3] = I'm full — note the 喇 marking a changed situation.

grammars.title: 想 and 要 — would like and want
body: Both can be translated “want” in English, but in Cantonese the gap is clear. [想|soeng2] is a **wish** that may not happen. [要|jiu3] is a **decision** already made — which is why 要 is what you use to order.

head: Sentence
Meaning
Nuance
rows: Just a thought, may not happen
[我想去日本|Ngo5 soeng2 heoi3 Jat6 bun2]。
I'd like to go to Japan.
[我要去日本|Ngo5 jiu3 heoi3 Jat6 bun2]。
I have to go to Japan.
[你想食咩呀|Nei5 soeng2 sik6 me1 aa3]？
What would you like to eat?
Do you want it or not?

after: **To negate: [唔想|m4 soeng2] (wouldn't like) and [唔要|m4 jiu3] (don't want).** To turn down an offer gently, the most natural choice is actually neither, but [唔使喇|m4 sai2 laa3] — “no need”.

🇭🇰 **When ordering, many Hongkongers drop the verb entirely.** [一杯凍檸茶，唔該|Jat1 bui1 dung3 ning4 caa4, m4 goi1]。 — one iced lemon tea, thanks. That's not lazy language; it's the most natural thing in a busy diner.

grammars.title: 鍾意 — like
body: [鍾意|zung1 ji3] covers both “like” and “love”. It can be followed by a noun or a verb, with no change of form at all.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: [我鍾意點心|Ngo5 zung1 ji3 dim2 sam1]。
[我好鍾意飲茶|Ngo5 hou2 zung1 ji3 jam2 caa4]。
[我唔鍾意辣|Ngo5 m4 zung1 ji3 laat6]。
[你鍾唔鍾意呀|Nei5 zung1 m4 zung1 ji3 aa3]？
[我最鍾意燒賣|Ngo5 zeoi3 zung1 ji3 siu1 maai2]。

after: **Look at the question form: [鍾唔鍾意|zung1 m4 zung1 ji3].** A two-syllable word is split — its first syllable is repeated with 唔 in between. This rule works for all two-syllable verbs: [識唔識|sik1 m4 sik1] (know or not), [知唔知|zi1 m4 zi1] (know or not), [鍾唔鍾意|zung1 m4 zung1 ji3].

⚠️ **[鍾意|zung1 ji3] about a person means liking in the romantic sense.** [我鍾意你|Ngo5 zung1 ji3 nei5] = I like you — and that's a serious statement. For “I like him” in the ordinary sense, use [佢好好人|keoi5 hou2 hou2 jan4] (he's a good person).

dialogs.title: 對話 2 — Invited to yum cha
dialogs.intro: Wong Lai invites Andi to yum cha for the first time. Yum cha is a social event, not just a meal — and its vocabulary alone is half of Hong Kong culture.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [聽日|Ting1 jat6][一齊去飲茶|jat1 cai4 heoi3 jam2 caa4]，[好唔好|hou2 m4 hou2]？
lines.id: Shall we go for yum cha tomorrow?
lines.literal: tomorrow — together — go — drink — tea, good — not — good.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [好呀|Hou2 aa3]！[我未飲過茶|Ngo5 mei6 jam2 gwo3 caa4]。
lines.id: Sure! I've never had yum cha.
lines.literal: good — huh. I — not-yet — drink — ever — tea.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [咁|Gam2][你想食|nei5 soeng2 sik6][咩點心|me1 dim2 sam1][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: So, what dim sum do you want?
lines.literal: so — you — would-like — eat — what — dim-sum — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我唔知|Ngo5 m4 zi1]，[你揀啦|nei5 gaan2 laa1]。
lines.id: I don't know — you choose.
lines.literal: I — not — know, you — choose — go-on.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [蝦餃|Haa1 gaau2]、[燒賣|siu1 maai2]、[叉燒包|caa1 siu1 baau1] — [呢三樣|ni1 saam1 joeng6][一定要食|jat1 ding6 jiu3 sik6]。
lines.id: Har gow, siu mai, char siu bao — these three are a must.
lines.literal: har-gow, siu-mai, char-siu — bun — these — three — kinds — definitely — must — eat.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [你鍾唔鍾意|Nei5 zung1 m4 zung1 ji3][腸粉|coeng2 fan2][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: Do you like cheung fun?
lines.literal: you — like — not — like — intestine — flour — huh.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [好鍾意|Hou2 zung1 ji3]！[我最鍾意|Ngo5 zeoi3 zung1 ji3][蝦腸|haa1 coeng2]。
lines.id: I love it! My favorite is shrimp cheung fun.
lines.literal: filler — like. I — most — like — shrimp — intestine.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我唔食得辣|Ngo5 m4 sik6 dak1 laat6]，[得唔得呀|dak1 m4 dak1 aa3]？
lines.id: I can't handle spicy food, is that OK?
lines.literal: I — not — eat — able — spicy, OK — not — OK — huh.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [冇問題|Mou5 man6 tai4]，[點心唔辣㗎|dim2 sam1 m4 laat6 gaa3]。
lines.id: No problem, dim sum isn't spicy anyway.
lines.literal: not-have — problem, dim-sum — not — spicy — emphasis.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [咁好啦|Gam2 hou2 laa1]。[幾點呀|Gei2 dim2 aa3]？
lines.id: Great, then. What time?
lines.literal: so — good — go-on. how-many — o'clock — huh.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [十點|Sap6 dim2]，[喺旺角等|hai2 Wong6 gok3 dang2]。[唔好遲到呀|M4 hou2 ci4 dou3 aa3]！
lines.id: Ten o'clock, meet in Mongkok. Don't be late!
lines.literal: ten — o'clock, at — Mongkok — wait. don't — late — huh.

notes: **[飲茶|jam2 caa4] literally means “drink tea”, but it means the whole event**: going to a restaurant in the morning or at midday, ordering basket after basket of dim sum, and sitting for hours. 🇭🇰 When someone invites you to 飲茶, they're not offering a cup of tea — they're inviting you to a meal together.

**[咁|gam2] at the start of a sentence = “so, then”.** It links what the other person just said to what you're about to say. ⚠️ Don't confuse it with tone-3 [咁|gam3], meaning “so …, that …”: [咁貴|gam3 gwai3] = that expensive. Same character, different tone, very different meaning.
**[揀|gaan2] = choose.** A native Cantonese word that Mandarin doesn't have (it uses 選). [你揀啦|Nei5 gaan2 laa1] = you choose — a phrase you'll say often as a beginner.
**[樣|joeng6] is the classifier for “kinds, types”.** [三樣嘢|saam1 joeng6 je5] = three kinds of things. [呢三樣|ni1 saam1 joeng6] = these three kinds.
**[一定|jat1 ding6] = definitely, must.** [一定要食|jat1 ding6 jiu3 sik6] = a must-try. Negative: [唔一定|m4 jat1 ding6] = not necessarily.

**[食得辣|sik6 dak1 laat6] = can handle spicy food.** The pattern verb + [得|dak1] + adjective means “able to do it to that degree”. [佢跑得快|Keoi5 paau2 dak1 faai3] = he runs fast. To negate, put 唔 before the verb: [唔食得辣|m4 sik6 dak1 laat6].

**[唔好|m4 hou2] + verb = “don't”.** [唔好遲到|M4 hou2 ci4 dou3] = don't be late; [唔好講嘢|M4 hou2 gong2 je5] = don't talk. ⚠️ This is different from [唔好|m4 hou2] meaning “not good”; what follows it makes the difference.

grammars.title: Inviting and responding to invitations
body: Invitations in Cantonese almost always end with an A-唔-A question or the particle 啦. Here are the most common forms, from the lightest to the most insistent.

head: Invitation
Meaning
Nuance
rows: [一齊去飲茶，好唔好|Jat1 cai4 heoi3 jam2 caa4, hou2 m4 hou2]？
Shall we go for yum cha?
Polite, leaves room to say no
[不如我哋去飲茶|Bat1 jyu4 ngo5 dei6 heoi3 jam2 caa4]。
How about we go for yum cha.

head: Responding
Meaning
rows: [唔得呀|M4 dak1 aa3]，[我要返工|ngo5 jiu3 faan1 gung1]。
I can't, I have to work.
[等我諗下先|Dang2 ngo5 nam2 haa5 sin1]。

after: **[不如|bat1 jyu4] is the gentlest way to suggest something.** Literally “not as good as”, but used exactly like “how about”. [不如聽日啦|Bat1 jyu4 ting1 jat6 laa1]。 = how about tomorrow instead.

🇭🇰 **A flat refusal is considered rude; give a reason.** [唔得呀|M4 dak1 aa3] on its own sounds cold. The natural thing is [唔得呀，我要返工|M4 dak1 aa3, ngo5 jiu3 faan1 gung1] — with a reason, even a vague one.

sections.title: Cha chaan teng: ordering like a local

blocks.text: 茶餐廳 *caa4 caan1 teng1* is a Hong Kong institution: a diner serving noodles, rice, toast, milk tea, and coffee within minutes. The menu is written in shorthand, the waiters talk fast, and locals order in sentences with almost no verbs.

head: Menu
Cantonese
What's in it
rows: Hong Kong's strong, creamy milk tea
Whole lemon slices pressed in the glass
Drunk when you have a sore throat

blocks.title: The secret language of the menu
items: [走甜|zau2 tim4] — no sugar. [少甜|siu2 tim4] — less sweet.
[走冰|zau2 bing1] — no ice. [少冰|siu2 bing1] — light ice.
[飛邊|fei1 bin1] — crusts cut off.
[加底|gaa1 dai2] — extra rice/noodles. [走青|zau2 ceng1] — no scallions.
[堂食|tong4 sik6] — eat in. [外賣|ngoi6 maai6] — takeout. The waiter will ask [堂食定外賣呀|Tong4 sik6 ding6 ngoi6 maai6 aa3]？
🇭🇰 [搭枱|daap3 toi2] — sharing a table with strangers. At busy times it's normal and you can't refuse; just nod.

sections.title: Yum cha: names you need to know

head: Dim sum
Cantonese
What's in it
rows: Pork and shrimp, open yellow wrapper
Steamed bun with sweet barbecued pork
Rice-noodle rolls; shrimp or meat filling
Sticky rice with chicken, wrapped in a lotus leaf
Braised in black bean sauce — literally “phoenix claws”
Rice porridge, often with fish or meat

head: At the table
Meaning
rows: What tea would you like? (answer: [普洱|pou2 nei2] / [香片|hoeng1 pin2] / [壽眉|sau6 mei4])
[唔該，一籠蝦餃|M4 goi1, jat1 lung4 haa1 gaau2]。
A basket of har gow, please.

blocks.title: Two table habits you should know
items: 🇭🇰 **Tapping the table with two fingers = thank you.** When someone pours tea into your cup, tap the table twice with your index and middle fingers. You don't need to say anything, and not tapping at all seems a bit cold.
**Teapot lid set ajar = more water, please.** Lift the lid and rest it on the rim of the pot; a waiter will come and refill it without you having to call.
[加一|gaa1 jat1] — a ten percent service charge, added automatically at larger restaurants. Cha chaan tengs usually don't have it, and Hongkongers generally don't tip beyond that.

Name the drink complete with extras (走甜, 少冰), the food with the right classifier (一碗, 一杯), then close with 唔該. After that, review prices from Unit 3: how much would you pay for that order?
